I am a licensed nurse at a number of long term care facilities in my region.

Working in a "home-like" environment. It doesn't necessarily feel like work the majority of the time because I am in these residents' home. It looks and feels like a home not a facility. I can wear street clothes and get into discussions with anything my resident's desire. Now that differs depending on who I am working with. In Dementia it is absolutely wondrous the ideas and situations a demented mind can come up with. Turning their past into reality and I engage them in a way that puts me into their "world".

Contrary to common belief, there is a lot more to being a nurse than just giving pills in a "nursing home".
I love that you are able to find something beautiful in the minds of the demented, and that you can make them happy by engaging with them as with any other normal person.

The approach and interaction is different in the sense that most times you cannot have a full engaging/rewarding conversation. The outcome won't be the same as if you are conversing with someone sound of mind. But it is the moments of joy that matter. When I learn about a resident's past and can bring up happy memories or funny incidents (for example a resident has a brother who is terrible at fishing so I always mention how the brother has gone fishing for the afternoon then we both laugh knowing he won't catch anything) that always leaves the person in a good mood.

I like to see it as puzzles that just need to be solved and once I find the right combination I can fully engage that resident in their own individual way.
That's a really beautiful approach, our world needs people like you :) Do you have a favorite person to talk to, or are they all simply different?

Naturally anyone who is prone to increased behaviors can be more difficult to interact with. It makes it more challenging and can be very mentally draining. More time is usually spent assessing these residents and identifying what triggers behaviors and how we can manage them before we can actually interact with them. In some cases a person suffering from dementia can flat out refuse even conversation and become physically aggressive. That's when, with the help of the doctor and pharmacist, we tinker with medications to find what works best. I am not always for just giving out pills like candy though I am not against it. I believe there is a happy medium that can be found when combining approach (GPA: gentle persuasive approach) and medication. I'll never "snow" someone.
